articles.title: New Jersey’s governor calls on her lieutenant governor to resign over ethics report
articles.summary: Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell’s “ethical lapses persisted despite multiple warnings and trainings.”
articles.body: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Thursday evening that she gave Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell “until tomorrow” to resign after an investigation found he had violated state ethics and harassment policy. “Today, I’m announcing the conclusion and findings of an independent investigation into allegations regarding Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell,” Sherrill wrote on X. “The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office. I’m calling for his resignation and giving him until tomorrow to do so.” The state said this month that it had hired a law firm to investigate allegations against Caldwell, a Democrat who was elected on the ticket with Sherrill last year, claiming that he had behaved inappropriately toward women. Sherrill said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses persisted despite multiple warnings and trainings.” “The substantiated finding of sexual harassment is extremely troubling. I’ve seen firsthand how a hostile culture can undermine everyone’s ability to succeed. It’s insidious and ruptures the trust within an organization,” she said. Sherrill said that the investigation “fully examined the evidence, followed the facts, and protected everyone’s privacy” and that Caldwell’s resignation “is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents.” Lawyers for Caldwell, who has denied the allegations, said in a statement Thursday night that they “strongly disputed the three findings in the investigation,” as its conclusions “go further than the evidence supports.” “This unnecessarily protracted and one-sided process lacked the requisite due process that should be afforded every citizen of this state,” said Thomas Calcagni, a lawyer for Caldwell. Calcagni said Caldwell was “not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations or offer readily identifiable witnesses who possessed more pertinent, first-hand knowledge of the events in question.” The 61-page report found that Caldwell sexually harassed a young female staffer and her friend. Caldwell was also found to have violated state ethics rules for using his office to try to promote a state employee whom he had a romantic relationship with “on multiple occasions,” without disclosing the relationship. He also violated ethics rules by making a practice of taking personal guests to ticketed events without providing payment or reimbursement for the tickets, the report said. State Senate Republican Leader Anthony M. Bucco said in a statement Thursday that the investigation’s findings were “deeply disappointing.” “This situation has gone on for far too long, and if he doesn’t agree to resign, the Legislature should follow the necessary protocols to resolve this matter once and for all,” Bucco said. Caldwell is only the fourth lieutenant governor in New Jersey history, as the role was established by referendum in 2005. It includes the responsibility of taking over as governor when the governor is away, which Caldwell has done numerous times since the investigation began. Caldwell is also New Jersey’s secretary of state, overseeing elections, a critical role as the midterm elections approach in November.

articles.title: US and China must act as responsible powers together, Xi says as Trump toasts friendship at state dinner
articles.summary: Trump said he and Xi had "never gotten along better" as he hosted the Chinese president at the lavish White House event.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump welcomed China's President Xi Jinping to the White House for a lavish state dinner where both leaders touted a new chapter in their friendship.

Xi said the countries "must act as responsible major countries to meet the expectations of our peoples" while Trump toasted a future of "harmony, peace and success" for both nations.

While both pledged to ensure stability between them, experts have cautioned Xi's visit is yet to yield obvious progress on pressing issues.

Billionaire business leaders, Trump administration officials and US tech CEOs were among the dinner's guests. Their arrival was marked, however, by protesters shouting from just outside, some of whom were arrested.

Addressing those gathered late on Thursday, Trump thanked Xi for making the long trip to the US, and said the relationship between the two men was strong.

"We've never gotten along better," Trump said.

He praised the long history of US-China relations, although he did take an unscripted detour to praise his ongoing ballroom project.

In the off-the-cuff moment, he said as a "special treat" the Chinese leader and his wife could be the first to enter the ballroom, which is still a year away from completion.

Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far

Trump and Xi come face-to-face as US and China battle to win the AI race

"Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkling, it's our honour to have you do so," he said.

He also presented Xi with a sculpture of a bald eagle, America's national symbol, saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America".

"We hope it will find a nice, wonderful place in Beijing. It's your honour," he said.

Trump added that he and First Lady Melania had participated in the design of the sculpture.

Xi meanwhile thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration", making them "feel truly at home".

He said the two leaders were "making history in our bilateral engagements".

"We agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," Xi said, adding that the two shared "sincere and in-depth exchanges" that would strengthen relations between the two countries.

Like Trump's, Xi's remarks were heavy on flattery, focusing on cultural ties and shared history between the US and China.

The relationship between the two countries was "forged in blood and fire" during the fight against Japan in World War Two, before being furthered during the "ping pong" diplomacy of the Nixon administration, he said.

Towards the end of his speech, Xi said the US and China's goals could be "mutually reinforcing". He urged both sides to explore a "new approach for major countries to get along".

When the BBC entered the dining hall for the dinner, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was standing over a table and appeared to be telling an entertaining story that had two others nearby barreled over with laughter.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was at another table, with a serious look on his face. His wife is sat beside him, with Jared Kushner and White House chief of staff Monica Crowley nearby.

The White House invited scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and other corporate executives.

Attendees included members of Trump's cabinet, as well as family members like his children Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany.

Bosses from the tech industry in attendance included Apple's Tim Cook, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.

Both Cook and Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi. As was Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government.

Other companies whose leaders were in attendance include General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance, ExxonMobil and more.

Social media mogul Mark Zuckerberg also attended, as well as Jeff Yaas, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok.

"Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more."

But one notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there.

The office of the First Lady Melania Trump, which planned the event, said the dinner menu would showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence".

For their first course guests enjoyed yellow squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta. The ate off red tablecloths - red being a symbol of luck and good fortune in China.

For their main course they dined on a sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and roasted eggplant.

Dessert featured the two leaders and their fellow diners tucking into vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit, with an accompanying ice cream "made with harvested White House honey".

The wine chosen by the first lady included Schramsberg Blanc De Noir - a nod to President Nixon's 1972 "Toast to Peace" with former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, when they used a bottle from the same vineyard.

Trump and Xi will begin their day with tea at the White House's Red Room with their wives.

The group then head to the US National Archives for a tour of the building and its exhibits.

Formally called the National Archives and Records Administration, the building holds some of the most important documents regarding the founding of the United States - including the US Constitution, the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights.

Xi and his wife will depart Washington later in the day.

articles.title: The Memo: Rising bond yields, mortgage rates deepening gloom for Trump’s GOP
articles.summary: Hard numbers on the economy are spelling new trouble for President Trump and the GOP in the midterm elections. They also presage difficulties for millions of Americans. The central issue is one that rarely commands headlines in normal times: bond yields. The bond market is enormous but, usually, sleepy. That has changed recently — including…
articles.body:
Hard numbers on the economy are spelling new trouble for President Trump and the GOP in the midterm elections. They also presage difficulties for millions of Americans.

The central issue is one that rarely commands headlines in normal times: bond yields.

The bond market is enormous but, usually, sleepy. That has changed recently — including with big new jolts this week.

On Wednesday, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note had its steepest one-day rise in more than a year. On Thursday, yields kept edging up.

As the stock-trading day closed, the yield on the 10-year note was 5.163 percent, which according to The Wall Street Journal was the highest rate in 19 years. The yield on the 30-year bond reached its highest level since 2004, according to Reuters.

Bond markets are not a typical conversation topic around the kitchen tables of America. But they might soon become one, because yields are of critical importance in setting rates for other types of borrowing that are more familiar to regular consumers — mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt. Some effects are already being seen. The average interest rate on a 30-year mortgage surpassed 7 percent this week.

In aggregate, it seems like a bleak scenario.

“Anytime the ‘boring’ bond market becomes an issue, it’s never good news,” Jared Bernstein, who served as the chair of then-President Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, told this column.

Bernstein, now a senior fellow at the liberal Center for American Progress, stressed that the current situation is far from an esoteric concern, given how many people are already struggling with the cost of living.

“It’s a really important point,” he said. “When we talk about affordability, we are usually referring to highly salient and visible prices in the economy — the price of gas, the price of groceries, the price of childcare. But there’s another price that matters to a lot of people: The price of money, the price of borrowing.”

First, the basics: The federal government’s outgoings have outstripped its revenues for more than two decades. The last time the national government ran a surplus was in fiscal 2001.

To finance the shortfall, the U.S. Treasury Department sells bonds. These are, at their most basic level, IOU slips where the government gets money instantly from the bond-buyer. In return, it promises to pay back the full amount at the end of the term while paying interest in the interim. The rate of interest is known as the yield.

Most mainstream economists agree that there are several factors fueling the rise in yields at the moment.

First, the war on Iran has added to existing inflationary pressure by pushing the price of oil upward. The benchmark price of Brent crude oil rose more than 3 percent Thursday and sat around $106 Thursday evening. Before the war began, it was around $70.

That’s meant pain at the pump for Americans — the average price of a gallon of regular gas Thursday was $4.48, according to AAA. It was just below $3 right before the war.

Second, there is a growing nervousness about the overall fiscal health of the federal government. To be sure, this has been a concern for many years. But the U.S. national debt broke through the $40 trillion barrier last month, putting an exclamation point on those worries.

The fiscal question also raises the specter of a negative spiral. Rising debt levels cause unease among investors, which spikes bond yields, which raises the cost of servicing the debt, which renews the cycle all over again.

Thirdly, there’s a new factor in the equation. Tech companies are financing build-outs related to artificial intelligence with a massive borrowing spree. In basic terms, that means the federal government has to compete harder to get would-be creditors to buy its debt rather than buying corporate bonds from, say, Meta or Alphabet.

“It’s a pretty noxious brew,” said Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “The proximate cause is the war, and inflation, and the Fed’s reaction to that. But there is also just a tsunami of debt being issued. And the government’s financial situation is dark and the prospects are that it’s likely to get darker.”

It’s important to stress that the nation is not necessarily galloping toward a financial apocalypse.

The U.S. economy has recently proven more resilient than some experts predicted, the unemployment rate is a manageable 4.1 percent, and in general the stock market has continued to perform very strongly.

Stocks have wavered in recent days, however, in part because of bond market worries. The major indexes were essentially flat Thursday, having fallen sharply Wednesday.

There is still significant optimism on Wall Street about AI’s potential. But large institutional investors could move money increasingly into bonds if rising yields make them think the level of risk inherent in equities is no longer worth it.

President Trump continues to evince enormous confidence in the U.S. economy, often referencing stock market gains and also making more general, if vague, claims about the nation’s “hotness.”

The stock market has indeed risen sharply over his tenure. But there is little evidence that the voters agree with him about the broader health of the economy.

An Economist/YouGov poll earlier this month indicated that just 25 percent of Americans believe the state of the economy is “excellent” or “good,” while 74 percent said it is either “fair” or “poor.”

In the polling averages maintained by RealClearPolitics, just 34 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the economy and an even lower 27 percent approve of his handling of inflation.

Bernstein, the former Biden adviser, argued that Republicans “are being deservedly slammed on affordability. If you believe the polls — and that is an ‘if’ — they are going to pay a price for that in the midterms.”

The argument may be expected, coming from someone so closely allied with the most recent Democratic president.

But it’s hard to argue against the idea that, so long as bond yields keep rising, the GOP’s midterm hopes are likely to fade.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Internal DOJ charts show agency bleeding staff as caseloads surge
articles.summary: A drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads, according to documents obtained by The Hill and NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. A series of charts, apparently inadvertently shared and then recalled, show how the number of attorneys within the civil division has plummeted under the Trump administration.…
articles.body:
A drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads, according to documents obtained by The Hill and NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

A series of charts, apparently inadvertently shared and then recalled, show how the number of attorneys within the civil division has plummeted under the Trump administration.

The charts substantiate a dynamic long suspected: that the Justice Department would not be able to swiftly replace a crew of veteran attorneys after a wave of firings and resignations.

Stacey Young, who founded the Justice Department alumni group Justice Connection, described the staff turnover as a “massive exodus.”

“The workload has skyrocketed, particularly in the civil division offices that have lost the most lawyers. So what we’re seeing is that the lawyers who are left are overworked, stressed out, many have lost those who led their office because they were pushed out by this administration. And because of the difficult circumstances under which they’re working, I expect that the rate of departures won’t slow down anytime soon,” she told The Hill.

“Putting out this data seems to me like a desperate cry for help. It seems like the civil division knows how badly it needs more funds to hire more lawyers to make up for the purge of longstanding experts that they caused.”

According to the Office of Personnel Management, the Justice Department has lost roughly 10,000 workers since the start of the Trump administration, a metric that includes component agencies like the FBI and the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

In graph after graph, the charts track data from the start of the Trump administration through August, showing a significant decline in civil division staff as caseloads have steadily ticked up.

DOJ did not respond to request for comment to this story.

One chart reviewing impact on each branch within the division detailed how caseload was skyrocketing — with work for the commercial litigation branch jumping a whopping 84 percent per attorney, while lawyers in the Office of Immigration Litigation saw their workload jump 63 percent.

Attorneys who work on appeals saw their caseloads jump 54 percent while lawyers in the federal programs branch — those who work on defending executive orders among other administration priorities — saw their workloads jump 44 percent.

The number of attorneys in the federal programs branch dropped from 113 to 71 just within the first few months of the Trump administration. A jump in cases has largely settled to around 1,000, but they are being handled by a diminished team.

Jennifer Ricketts, a former Justice Department attorney who led the federal programs branch, said the swift exodus shows how many longtime attorneys who defended presidential priorities across administrations likely began looking for a new job as soon as President Trump won the election.

“They were aware of how much in the first Trump administration they tried to stretch the law and put us in positions where we struggled to make sure we satisfied our professional responsibilities and folks did not want to have to go through that exercise again,” she said of the branch.

“You don’t get jobs really quickly. So they had already started looking after the election, so it was not tied to any specific decision. It was the anticipation of what they may do, especially given how aggressive they said they were going to be and how aggressive we had seen them be in Trump one …. I think folks knew maybe not the scope of what was coming, but they knew none of it was going to be pleasant.”

One of the other most significant declines in staffing — combined with one of the highest rises in cases — was in the Office of Immigration Litigation, which has seen cases surge amid Trump’s pledge to carry out the largest mass deportation operation in history.

The Office of Immigration Litigation handles both individual immigration cases being heard at the Board of Immigration Appeals as well as immigration matters brought in federal district court, such as habeas corpus cases brought by migrants being held in detention. Habeas petitions have soared alongside detention rates as the administration has largely cut off access to bond hearings.

One former staffer from the immigration office noted the steady decline in staff in that branch, with attorneys going from 320 down to 243 as cases climbed from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500.

“We never had attrition like we’ve had. There’s been a lot of reasons for that,” the former staffer said.

Early in the administration, the Justice Department moved the branch’s leader to a new sanctuary city task force, and the Justice Department later made headlines for firing Erez Reuveni, a longtime Office of Immigration Litigation staffer, after he acknowledged in court that Kilmar Abrego Garcia had been mistakenly deported.

“When our colleague Erez Reuveni got fired, I think there were a lot of people that were saying, ‘If that could happen to him that could happen to any of us,’” the former staffer continued. “And I think that people just started looking, and you know, workload’s gone up. The office has sort of tried to recover from those blows … But it’s been increasingly challenging for people to do that. I think there’s a lot of unhappy people.”

“With caseload going up and the resources going down, it just makes it challenging,” they added.

Also surprising is the attrition among appellate staff attorneys, though their ranks have been rising over the last several months.

“It’s a very plum section, very elite section, and if folks leave there, they would often go to the solicitor general’s office or some other very prestigious placement,” Ricketts said, referencing the team of attorneys for the solicitor who argue before the Supreme Court.

While staffing in that branch hasn’t dipped as much as others, their caseload has increased substantially because the Trump administration has been appealing so many of its losses in court.

Though now down six attorneys from the 61 it began with, the number of appealed cases went from around 780 at the start of the administration to more than 1,100 last month.

“They will appeal everything. I mean, it does not appear to be an administration that takes losses. They do not seem to be worried about creating bad law in the court of appeals. They seem to be pursuing a very aggressive interpretation of executive branch authority, and so they are willing to roll the dice and take it up,” Ricketts said.

“I think my sense is they have a sense that the Supreme Court is willing to accept more of those ideas, what would have been considered extreme ideas, than we ever imagined, and so why not?”

Similarly to the Office of Immigration Litigation, the commercial litigation branch has also seen a consistent loss in staff — dropping from 350 at the start of the administration down to 289 — while caseloads have jumped from around 13,000 to nearly 19,000.

It’s hard to know what has driven the surge in caseload in the branch, which handles a wide variety of matters from cases where the government has a financial interest to intellectual property to those who represent the U.S. in cases in foreign courts.

But it does include two areas where there has been more active litigation.

The commercial litigation branch includes fraud — a topic of great interest to the Trump administration as it probes entitlement programs.

It also handles cases before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the quasi judicial board responsible for reviewing federal employee workplace challenges, including wrongful termination cases that have surged as the Trump administration pushed to reduce the size of the government.

After the email with the charts was sent last week, it was quickly recalled.

Sources suspect the graphs are preparation for the next budget cycle.

“Somewhere along the line, somebody in the division or the department is going to use this data to justify asking for more resources,” the former Office of Immigration Litigation staffer said.

They noted that none of the graphs start its axis at zero, a choice that emphasizes the rise in cases and fall in staff.

“They ginned up the charts to make that visually apparent,” they said.

The Justice Department has already made efforts to recruit more staff. In May, the department promised something largely unheard of in the federal government — a $25,000 signing bonus to those joining the civil division.

The Justice Department “had never given signing bonuses to try to attract applicants. These jobs were some of the most competitive legal jobs in the field. The fact that they’re now having to provide financial incentives for people to apply shows you just how desperate they are,” Young said.

“And we know that job openings that used to attract hundreds or thousands of applications are now attracting almost none.”

The Justice Department took a number of actions shortly after Trump took office that flushed staff and prompted headlines.

In the criminal division, the Justice Department fired those who had worked on cases involving Trump. In the civil division, many branch leaders were reassigned to take on unrelated work. The U.S. pardon attorney lost her job after she refused to certify that actor Mel Gibson should have his gun rights restored. And still more attorneys sought and gained jobs outside the department or availed themselves of a government buyout spearheaded by Elon Musk.

At the beginning of the administration, the Justice Department also withdrew offers to recent graduates who had been given entry level jobs through the prestigious Attorney General’s Honors Program, cutting off a pipeline of young attorneys from top schools who then rise through the ranks of the department.

“It reflects what we’ve been saying all along. This situation is untenable when you have an office that is experiencing a surge of cases because of this administration’s lawless conduct at a time when lawyers are fleeing the department. The administration won’t be able to defend itself in court,” Young said.

“DOJ lawyers, in the best of times, are overworked. Their workloads right now have increased exponentially, especially when it comes to civil division lawyers, and as their workloads continue to increase, more will leave, and the problem will just keep getting worse and worse.”

articles.title: GOP senators dismayed by Trump embrace of Xi after China helped Iran target US troops
articles.summary: Republican senators are expressing concern and dismay over President Trump’s lavish welcome of Chinese President Xi Jinping to a two-day summit in Washington after it was revealed earlier this month that Iran used Chinese satellite imagery to target U.S. troops in Jordan. Republican senators were told of deepening military cooperation between Iran and China at…
articles.body:
Republican senators are expressing concern and dismay over President Trump’s lavish welcome of Chinese President Xi Jinping to a two-day summit in Washington after it was revealed earlier this month that Iran used Chinese satellite imagery to target U.S. troops in Jordan.

Republican senators were told of deepening military cooperation between Iran and China at a closed-door national security briefing Thursday, heightening their concerns about Trump’s red-carpet welcome of Xi at Joint Base Andrews.

GOP lawmakers called on Trump to confront Xi over reports that China has provided military assistance to Iran and demanded that China produce real concessions on trade, especially U.S. agricultural exports, concessions that have been elusive in Trump’s negotiations with China.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said the 21-gun salute and B-1 bomber flyover that greeted Xi’s arrival were “over the top.”

“The summit has been planned for a long time,” she said. “Is it appropriate that you welcome him? Yeah. But it’s equally appropriate that you ask him really tough questions.”

She said the military honors for Xi were excessive.

“Personally, I felt that the 21-cannon volley and the red carpet was a little bit over the top — the flyover. I don’t think we need to do that,” she said.

Republican senators are also questioning Trump’s invitation of Russian President Vladimir Putin to the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December. Trump announced it earlier this week.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said he wasn’t happy to see Trump lavish Xi with honors given escalating tensions between the U.S. and China over the war in Iran, Taiwan’s independence and the artificial intelligence race.

“I understand the importance of engagement and diplomacy but inviting Putin to the G20 and rolling out the red carpet for President Xi, I’m not enthusiastic about that,” he said.

Cornyn, a member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said it’s “pretty clear” that China, Russia, Iran and North Korea have formed an “axis” alliance opposed to the United States.

“We’ve seen that happen before with disastrous consequences, so I think we need to be very concerned and very aware of what’s happening,” he warned.

Cornyn also balked at Trump’s entreaty to Putin to attend the G20 meeting in Miami later this year.

“I think the president needs a reset with Putin,” he said, arguing that Trump doesn’t recognize “Putin as the stone-cold killer that he is.”

Anna Kelly, a White House spokesperson, said Trump is “reciprocating” the hospitality that Xi showed the president when he visited Beijing in May.

“President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week,” Kelly said.

“The President will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people,” the spokesperson added.

Trump on Thursday hailed a “truly great friendship” with Xi to start the two-day summit. Xi struck a more measured tone but emphasized the interests of China and the U.S. “are deeply intertwined.”

The two leaders met for nearly three hours at the White House and were scheduled to attend a state dinner Thursday evening.

Xi made a diplomatic gesture by announcing that China will send two pandas to the Atlanta zoo and would extend invitations to 100,000 U.S. students to study in China.

But those offerings were overshadowed by a briefing senators received Thursday about growing military cooperation between Chinese and Iranian national security forces, which may have increased the lethal accuracy of Iranian strikes on U.S. and allied targets.

“I just left a classified briefing on the defense budget leaving me shocked and deeply alarmed about what China is doing to aid Iran, which is seeking to kill our military men and women,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said. “I think the American people should be shocked.

“President Trump should be saying to Xi, ‘Stop it, knock it off,’ rather than feting and welcoming him in this elaborate way,” he said.

Other Republican senators called on Trump to confront Xi over growing military cooperation with Iran amid the conflict with U.S. forces in the Middle East.

“I would certainly hope [Trump] would bring that up [with Xi] and let him know U.S. disappointment and that has consequences,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said.

Curtis also urged Trump to reconsider his outreach to Putin. The Utah senator said he’s “not a fan” of that decision.

“We need to clarify who our friends are and who our enemies are,” he said.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he saw public media reporting that Iran used Chinese satellite imagery in a strike that killed three U.S. service members in Jordan.

He said he “hopes” Trump “brings up the topic” of Chinese military assistance to Iran during the summit.

“It’s fine he’s here, and it’s fine that he treats him like a foreign leader, but it’s also important that he confronts these issues with him,” he said.

Cramer said Trump has to be “really strong” with China over national security concerns, such as military cooperation with Iran and how it intercepted sensitive F-35 strike fighter parts.

The Pentagon is investigating how China obtained parts of one the U.S.’s most advanced fighter jets, according to The Associated Press. Congress is also investigating the diversion of the strike-fighter equipment to Hong Kong.

Cramer said Trump is “plenty capable of being tough” when he wants to be.

The North Dakota Republican said Trump should get tough with Putin as well.

Asked about the president’s invitation to Putin to the G20 summit, Cramer replied: “I think he’s giving Vladimir Putin more credit than he deserves.”

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), the Senate Armed Services Committee chair, slammed Xi during a floor speech Tuesday when he suggested that Trump should “not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome.”

Wicker suggested, tongue in cheek, that Trump “might inquire” of Xi during the fancy state dinner “about the purposes of China’s massive military buildup or about China’s clear support for Iran.”

“It was all over the press that China gave Iran satellite imagery intelligence and that led to the death of American troops. So, I would certainly suggest that the president try to get an answer to that,” he said.

Kelly, the White House spokesperson, disputed the claim that China has enhanced Iran’s ability to target American forces.

“As the President stated, nothing that any outside actor is doing to help Iran is in any way increasing their ability to target Americans,” she said.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), however, said he shares the concerns expressed by Wicker and other GOP colleagues over the pomp surrounding Trump’s reception of Xi.

“We should be having those sorts of reception for people who are not plotting our ultimate demise — not Xi Jinping,” he said.

articles.title: Why the Lindsay Clancy case terrifies me for America’s future
articles.summary: What frightens me most is that my son will grow up in a country that is learning to confuse empathy for justice.
articles.body:
I have spent my career as a statistician telling people not to get emotional about numbers. This week, I’m breaking my own rule.

Our son is 13 months old. He has just figured out how to walk, which means he has also figured out how to fall. I spend most of my day catching him. So forgive me if I couldn’t read the coverage of the Lindsay Clancy trial with the cool detachment of a statistician.

In January 2023, Clancy strangled her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan, in their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts. This is not disputed — her defense team never asserted that she didn’t do it. Rather, they argued that postpartum psychosis made her not criminally responsible.

After a seven-week trial and 85 witnesses, 11 of 12 jurors agreed with this defense. One man held out, and on Sept. 4 the judge declared a mistrial.

Now let’s look at the numbers, because that’s what I do.

YouGov asked more than 23,000 Americans what the right verdict would be. Among men, 51 percent said guilty of murder. Fifteen percent said not guilty by reason of insanity. Among women, it was 41 percent guilty and 26 percent not guilty. Among Democratic women , only 27 percent viewed it as murder.

I’m a statistician before I’m a columnist, so let me be fair. A 10-point gender gap is not the war of the sexes some corners of the internet have made it out to be. Most women did not side with Clancy, and “guilty” was still the most common answer among women overall. But when more than one in four women in this country can look at a mother who strangled three little children and conclude she shouldn’t be held responsible, that isn’t a rounding error — that’s a signal.

And no, I’m not dismissing postpartum mental illness. I have lived through the sleepless haze of the first year, and struggling mothers deserve far more help than they get. But compassion for an illness and absolution for an act of murder are two very different things. We seem to have lost the ability to tell them apart.

That to me, is what’s wrong with America right now.

Start with the number that surprised me most. It wasn’t the gender gap. It was the party gap .

Sixty-one percent of Republicans said Clancy was guilty of murder. Among Democrats, it was 34 percent. That’s a 27-point gap, nearly three times the gap between men and women. Three children were strangled in their home, and somehow even that got sorted along party lines.

When the killing of an 8-month-old becomes a question you answer by checking your team, we’ve lost something we can’t poll our way back to.

Part of what we have lost is a shared moral vocabulary. We used to have words like “wrong,” “guilty” and “responsible,” and we used them without apologizing. Now, we reach for clinical language instead. We talk about “trauma,” “triggers” and “systems.” Diagnosis has quietly displaced judgment.

Mental illness is real, and the law rightly makes room for it. But when every terrible act gets explained by a condition, no one is ever responsible for anything. And a society where no one is responsible can’t protect anyone.

We have become a country where feelings count as evidence. There are countless other examples. Take Luigi Mangione and the murder of the United Health Care CEO Brian Thompson. But this one just goes too far. The most sympathetic story in the room wins, and the question “Who is the victim?” gets answered by whoever has the most compelling narrative, not by innocents who lost their lives.

Cora, Dawson and Callan don’t have a legal team or a narrative. They don’t have a hashtag or a team of experts explaining their inner world. Somehow, in so much of this conversation, they became supporting characters in their killer mother’s victim narrative.

We have also lost our nerve about personal responsibility. Context matters; I spend my whole life adding context to numbers. But when context becomes a universal excuse, accountability starts to sound like cruelty, and judgment starts to sound like bigotry.

Look at how we have treated the holdout. He has been publicly criticized by his fellow jurors for refusing to go along, doxxed by the larger community and is now even being investigated. The lone dissenter is exactly who the jury system was designed to protect, yet society has recast this hero as the villain.

As a mother, what frightens me most is that my son will grow up in a country that is learning to confuse empathy for justice. Empathy is a beautiful instinct, but a society that pours its sympathy onto the person who did the killing, while the children who died become an afterthought, has its moral math backwards.

I tell my students that data never tells you what to feel — it tells you where to look. These numbers are telling us to look hard at ourselves.

When I put my son to bed tonight, I will be thinking about three children in Duxbury who deserved someone to speak for them.

The least the rest of us can do is remember their names.

Dr. Liberty Vittert Capito is professor at the Olin Business School at Washington University in St. Louis .

articles.title: Senate map stretches in both directions
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Senate battleground map expands ▪ Trump, Xi exchange gifts ▪ Journalists allowed back in White House ▪ Mortgage, bond market concerns The Senate map appears to be widening, with more states in play for both parties just a little more than five weeks out from the midterms. The nonpartisan election handicapper…
articles.body:
▪ Journalists allowed back in White House

The Senate map appears to be widening, with more states in play for both parties just a little more than five weeks out from the midterms.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report this week shifted two GOP strongholds in Democrats’ direction, moving Kansas from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican” and South Carolina from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican.”

Republicans, meanwhile, are liking their chances this year in New Hampshire and Minnesota: Cook Political Report last week shifted New Hampshire toward Republicans, from “lean Democrat” to “toss-up,” and the scant polling in Minnesota points to a highly competitive race, with the latest KSTP/SurveyUSA poll showing the Democratic nominee, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan , and Republican Michele Tafoya tied at 42 percent.

RealClearPolitics also moved three states into the “toss-up” category this past week, shifting New Hampshire and Minnesota toward Republicans, and Kansas toward Democrats.

These states add to a battleground map that includes Maine, Iowa, Alaska, Michigan and Ohio. Georgia and North Carolina are seen as becoming increasingly difficult for Republicans, while Nebraska remains a longshot as independent Dan Osborn looks to knock off Sen. Pete Ricketts (R).

The overall political environment favors Democrats going into November, with President Trump notching record-low approval ratings amid the Iran war and sky-high gas prices, and Democrats holding a double-digit advantage on the generic congressional ballot, according to the latest polls.

But candidate quality is also proving to be a factor as the Senate map widens. In New Hampshire, where Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is retiring, Republicans convinced former Sen. John E. Sununu (R-N.H.), a member of the state’s popular political dynasty, to run for the Senate against Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.).

Sununu has distanced himself from the president but has nonetheless earned his endorsement, potentially satisfying both MAGA voters and never-Trump Republicans.

“Even in a light blue state, the amount of money national Republicans have dedicated to this race is a flashing red light for Democrats,” Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote in an analysis of the race last week.

Candidate quality also seems to be shaping the race in South Carolina, where Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) was tapped this summer to fill her late brother’s seat and is now running for a full term in the upper chamber.

After eking out a win in the GOP special election primary, Graham is still plagued by some of the same challenges, including unsteady debate performances and criticism over being elevated to the job because of her family name. She faces Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews , who’s been running ads targeting centrist and GOP-leaning voters.

“To be clear, Graham remains the heavy favorite,” Cook wrote of the race. “It’s still incumbent upon Andrews to prove she can get out of the mid-40s polling — always a hurdle in South Carolina — and make this a truly competitive race.”

Meanwhile, in Kansas, Democrats have gone on the attack, seizing on reporting that questions the debt collection lawsuits allegedly filed by Republican Sen. Roger Marshall ’s former OB-GYN practice. He also faces a formidable opponent in Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton .

But Democrats also see Kansas as increasingly within reach for economic issues. Agriculture is a major factor in the state, and high fuel and fertilizer prices have squeezed many voters in the state.

“We see this as an increasingly worrisome contest for the GOP that should be called competitive at this juncture, though one where Republicans still have the edge,” Taylor wrote about Kansas in Wednesday’s analysis.

Minnesota has consistently had close races, but a Republican hasn’t won statewide in two decades. But after the progressive lieutenant governor defeated centrist Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.) in the Democratic primary, Republicans see cause for optimism.

Minnesota Public Radio reports the race is oddly quiet just weeks out from election day. That may change as polls show Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster, has a fighting chance.

▪ The Hill : Democrats leading in Michigan, New Hampshire Senate races: Survey.

▪ The Hill : Marshall GOP primary challenger backs Democrat in Kansas Senate race.

Trump honored Chinese leader Xi Jinping at last night’s state dinner, after they held meetings throughout the day . There’s always a host of issues at the forefront between the U.S. and China, but NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman says we shouldn’t forget the ongoing space race. I asked Isaacman which nation is leading at this point in time.

“They will absolutely do what the Soviets never could during the first space race,” Isaacman told me of China. “They intend to put their astronauts on the surface of the moon in 2029. Our intention is to do it in 2028. That means no matter what, it’s coming down to months, not years. That is way too close.”

Keep in mind a year ago when we were talking about Trump and Xi, the conversation was about tariffs and trade, and not AI. We’ll have to see if outer space becomes the next frontier in the ongoing competition between the two countries.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

The Department of Homeland Security asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume deporting immigrants to countries they have no ties to, known as third-country removals. It comes after an appeals court ordered the flights to stop without giving those facing deportation a better opportunity to raise claims they’ll face torture.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a defiant speech before the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, defending Israel’s actions against Iran and attacking New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Dozens of delegates walked out during the speech.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed Thursday that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is “completely” healthy despite reports that he could be in significantly poor health following the initial U.S.-Israeli airstrikes that launched the war in February. Khamenei hasn’t been seen in public since becoming supreme leader.

President Donald Trump shakes hands with China’s President Xi Jinping during a State Dinner in the East Room of the White House, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

PLACE TO BE : The first full day of Chinese President Xi Jinping ’s visit concluded with a state dinner last night that featured a gift from Trump and a who’s who of Big Tech leaders.

The dinner featured an extensive guest list , including members of the Cabinet, a few Supreme Court justices, media figures and members of Trump’s family. Also present were some of the most powerful business leaders — Meta CEO Mark Zuckerburg , OpenAI head Sam Altman , Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos .

Trump had brought several of them with him for his trip to China back in May, emphasizing his view of the importance of their role in the U.S.-China relationship.

The dinner capped a day of pomp and bilateral talks between the two powers. Trump presented Xi with a bald eagle statute as a gift to bring back to China during his remarks.

That came after Xi announced earlier in the day that he was gifting the U.S. with two giant pandas and invitations for 100,000 U.S. students to study in China over the next five years.

“The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and the Americans,” Xi said, referencing the longstanding “panda diplomacy” that was key to improving U.S.-Chinese relations decades earlier.

The day wasn’t without significant protests against Xi’s visit. A large group of protesters rallied outside the White House during the day and at night against the Chinese Communist Party leader.

“Xi Jinping you’re not welcome,” one chant could be heard.

▪ The Hill : GOP senators dismayed by Trump’s embrace of Xi.

▪ CNN : Trump-Xi meeting heavy on pomp, light on substance.

BACK IN THE BUILDING : Journalists for CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back onto White House grounds Thursday following a federal judge’s ruling blocking Trump from banning the outlets.

The banned outlets reported that their journalists and photographers were initially still denied access to the White House early in the day despite the order, leading their attorneys to petition the judge to compel the Trump administration to comply. Their reporters were ultimately allowed into the building soon after.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly , a Trump appointee, ruled in the early morning hours Thursday that the administration must restore access to the outlets, finding the bans were instituted without due process, as required by longstanding judicial precedent. Kelly’s ruling is valid for 14 days.

Trump has suggested ahead of the ruling that he expected to lose and would appeal, though he hasn’t directly responded to the ruling yet. He did slam CNN and MS NOW in a Truth Social post for not covering the “made for” TV event of Xi’s visit.

The status of the White House television pool remains in limbo. Journalists from multiple outlets were on hand ready to cover Xi’s visit, but they continued their boycott of the press pool given the uncertainty surrounding whether the White House would allow CNN to rejoin the rotation, The Hill’s Julia Manchester reports . The five-member TV pool includes CNN, Fox News and the three major broadcast networks.

▪ The Washington Post : White House banned Politico citing its own quotes.

WATCH OUT : Economic warning signs are flashing as the war in Iran and Trump’s trade policies fuel more anxiety.

The average 30-year mortgage rate surpassed 7 percent Thursday, the first time it has done so since January 2025, just before Trump came back into office. The Hill’s Max Rego reports that this marks the fifth consecutive weekly rise in mortgage rates.

The rates still have room to go before reaching the 25-year high of 7.79 percent that was recorded in October 2023, but analysts expect the cost of borrowing to remain high with inflation above the Federal Reserve’s target and the war driving up energy prices.

Meanwhile, the bond market is continuing to set new high marks. The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond yield hit its highest point since 2007 on Wednesday at 5.13 percent, while the 30-year bond yield hit a two-decade intraday high of 5.45 percent on Thursday.

The Hill’s Niall Stanage reports for Insider about how the rise in the bond market is becoming more and more of an issue, even as public attention is on more colorful topics. Read more about why the bond market is sparking concerns and what it could mean for consumers and the battle for the midterms here .

▪ CBS News : What the bond market freaking out means for your money.

NARROW DEFEAT : Another war powers resolution directing the president to withdraw troops from the Iran conflict narrowly failed in the Senate on Thursday as four Republicans joined almost all Democrats in favor.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) voted in favor of the resolution for the first time, joining fellow Republican Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Rand Paul (Ky.), leading to a 49-50 vote. Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.) was the only Senate Democrat to oppose the measure.

Tillis said he flipped his vote because the war has dragged on for too long without congressional authorization, also arguing that it has become a political liability for Republican candidates.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) seemed undecided ahead of the vote but ultimately cast his vote against it. He and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) were meeting just off the Senate floor right before Cassidy voted no.

The vote comes as some GOP candidates and lawmakers have started to break with the president on the war as polls show dwindling support.

▪ The Hill Insider : Pentagon turns on the jets in $1.5 trillion budget push.

▪ The Hill : Bipartisan lawmakers announce U.S. film incentive package.

The president and first lady will greet the Chinese president and his wife for tea at 10:35 a.m. They will visit the National Archives together at 11:30 a.m. He will participate in signing time at 4:30 p.m.

The U.S. Department of Justice logo is seen on a podium before a news conference, May 4, 2026, in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press)

SHORT STAFFED: A drastically diminished workforce at the Department of Justice (DOJ) is struggling to keep up with its civil caseload after a wave of firings and departures of veteran attorneys during the Trump administration, according to documents obtained by The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch and NewsNation’s Samuel Marks .

The number of attorneys in the civil division has plummeted under Trump, the documents show, substantiating longstanding concerns that the DOJ would have trouble replacing the attorneys that left earlier in the president’s term.

A series of graphs — which appeared to be inadvertently shared and then recalled — track data showing a decline in civil division staff just as caseloads pick up.

One chart showed how caseload was skyrocketing on each branch: Workload jumped a whopping 84 percent per attorney in the commercial litigation branch and increased by 63 percent for lawyers working in the Office of Immigration Litigation.

The DOJ has lost roughly 10,000 workers since Trump took office, according to the Office of Personnel Management. That number includes staff in component agencies of the DOJ, like the FBI and the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

Stacey Young , founder of the Justice Department alumni group Justice Connection, described the staff turnover as a “massive exodus” and said she doesn’t expect the departures to slow down in the near future.

“Putting out this data seems to me like a desperate cry for help,” she told Beitsch. “It seems like the civil division knows how badly it needs more funds to hire more lawyers to make up for the purge of longstanding experts that they caused.”

▪ Reuters : Trump says DOJ could rein in AI companies.

▪ CBS News : DOJ says it’s moving to end 50 school desegregation cases.

Florida gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) speaks at the Republican convention on Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas. (Julio Cortez, Associated Press)

THROWBACK : There’s increasing signs that Florida may be returning — for this cycle, at least — to the battleground status that it held for years before it turned into solid Republican territory during the Trump era.

In one of the most high-profile signs of the shift, Decision Desk HQ shifted the Florida governor’s race from “leans Republican” to “toss-up” on Wednesday. Rep. Byron Donalds , the Republican nominee, currently has a 59 percent chance of winning the race against Democratic nominee and former Rep. David Jolly in the forecast.

While Donalds is still the favorite, even a somewhat close race on Election Day would mark a significant shift for the state after outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) won reelection by nearly 20 points in 2022.

Donalds also received attention this week after his campaign website removed multiple mentions of the president, making him one of several Republicans who have seemed to distance themselves in recent weeks. Donalds called Trump’s agenda “common sense” when pressed about the changes.

He’s not the only Florida Republican who made a notable move involving Trump recently.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar turned heads last week when she released an ad accusing Trump of having gone “too far” in his administration’s immigration crackdown. Salazar represents a red-leaning district, but forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted its rating of her race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican” this week.

Fox News shifted 15 House races away from Republicans this week, including four contests in Florida. That included moving Rep. Anna Paulina Luna ’s race from “Likely R” to “Lean R” and Rep. Kathy Castor ’s race from “Lean R” to “Toss Up.” Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz ’s district was shifted from “Toss Up” to “Lean D.”

At the same time, Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon is hoping to pull off an upset against Sen. Ashley Moody (R). One poll from last week showed them essentially tied , a surprising result in a state where Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in more than a decade.

Still, another poll out this week showed the Republicans with much more comfortable leads in both the governor and Senate races.

Attacks and threats against federal judges have spiked, and it threatens our democracy , Judge Shira Scheindlin writes in The Hill.

The diesel export ban folly , Mike Sommers writes in The Wall Street Journal.

CNN Senior Reporter Betsy Klein walks through the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington. (Alex Brandon, Associated Press)

And finally … 👏👏👏 Congrats to this week’s Morning Report quiz winners ! They were on the scene with answers about the White House press pool.

Here’s who went 4/4: Stan Wasser, Michael Salanik, Chuck Schoenenberger, Harry Strulovici, Sari Wisch, Tom Chabot, Rick Schmidtke, Richard Baznik, Linda L. Field, Leslie Hurst, Ned Sauthoff, Linda Kavalsky, Jenessa Wagner, M. Whitehouse, Terry Pflaumer, Carmine Petracca and Dan Beierman .

Lore states that Teddy Roosevelt invited reporters into the White House after seeing them out in a rainstorm. While that story is likely just legend, Roosevelt did revolutionize how the president interacted with the press.

The first Trump administration briefly removed the credentials of Jim Acosta after he and a staffer struggled over a microphone when Acosta was questioning the president. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who also ruled in the current case, ordered Acosta’s credentials to be restored , and the White House dropped its push.

No journalists were kicked out of the press pool during Joe Biden’s presidency. In 2023, the White House revised its policy to require credentialed journalists to reapply. articles.title: The Pentagon should remember the value of professional dissent
articles.summary: It is especially important for military institutions tasked with fighting wars and expending the nation’s blood and treasure through conflict.
articles.body:
Professional dissent can drive innovation and offer differing points of view for the leadership of the institutions in which we serve and work. It is especially important for military institutions tasked with fighting wars and expending the nation’s blood and treasure through conflict.

Today, there is reportedly a fear that exists within the U.S. Department of Defense. Highly qualified officers are being pulled off of promotion lists for vague and unclear reasons. Army senior leaders have been fired for reportedly not aligning themselves with the ideological aims and culture wars of current Defense Department leadership.

The ripple effect is that this fear can inhibit dissent within the American military, especially because it needed today during the U.S conflict against Iran.

For a time in my career, I was a prominent critic of the U.S. military’s counterinsurgency doctrine and of U.S. strategy in Iraq and Afghanistan. From 2007 to 2013, I wrote commentaries and gave public speeches and lectures to military and civilian audiences directed at the U.S. Army and Department of Defense.

As a serving Army officer, I was careful to stay within my lane. I did not question policy decisions made by American presidents in both wars, such as President George W. Bush’s decision to invade Iraq in 2003 and then stay and occupy the country for eight years or President Obama’s decision to “surge” additional troops into Afghanistan in 2012.

Still, it was clear that my efforts during those years ruffled a lot of feathers in the ranks of army officers and likely in the Defense Department. That’s because I said that their operational approaches in Iraq and Afghanistan and their larger military strategies were not working. In 2012, I went so far as to say that the United States deserved an F grade for its failing strategy in Afghanistan.

But not once did senior leaders tell me to shut up and to stop producing professional dissent. Thinking back on those times, it is encouraging to remember that the U.S. military — from the Pentagon to U.S. Army leadership — tolerated my dissent, even if many of those leaders disagreed with it, some of them stridently.

It is hard to imagine a current U.S. service member offering similar criticism toward the operations against Iran. In this Department of Defense’s atmosphere of fear — where U.S. military officers and civilians are being polygraphed for allegedly leaking sensitive information — consider what might happen if an officer published an essay criticizing the operations against Iran and asking hard questions on whether they are achieving U.S. objectives.

A serving officer criticizing an operational approach or military strategy is different from criticizing the policy and actions of a presidential administration. Gen. Douglas McArthur did exactly that in early 1951 during the Korean War, when he publicly argued for taking the war to the Chinese homeland and possibly using nuclear weapons against China. That was not professional military dissent; it was disobedience and an outright challenge to policy. President Harry Truman was right for relieving McArthur because of it.

In 2008, when my promotion packet was in front of the selection board that could promote me from lieutenant colonel to full colonel, a Wall Street Journal reporter wrote an article titled “Officer Questions Petraeus’s Strategy” on my early criticism of the army’s counterinsurgency under Gen. David H. Petraeus.

It never occurred to me that my professional dissent could somehow hurt my chances for promotion to colonel. I trusted that the promotion board would base its decision on my performance as a lieutenant colonel in combat during the invasion of Iraq in 2003 and when in command of a cavalry squadron in west Baghdad in 2006.

As I expected, the board based its decision on my performance in combat, and fortunately, I was promoted to colonel.

With the war against Iran entering its seventh month , along with the likelihood of future U.S. military conflicts, it is especially important today and in the future for the Department of Defense to allow service members to express professional military dissent without damaging repercussions.

History offers a compelling example. In March 1968 during the Tet Offensive in the Vietnam War, Army helicopter pilot Warrant Officer Hugh Thompson Jr. saw the killing of innocent civilians in the village of My Lai. He reported his observations to senior leaders, which eventually led to a full investigation.

Hopefully, the Department of Defense will embrace the spirit of professional dissent from today’s service members to ensure the intellectual baseline for an effective, moral and ethically driven U.S. military.

Gian Gentile is a retired U.S. Army colonel and former director of the military history program at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: Trump plays the hits, but struggling GOP seeks new material
articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 am ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!] There are a couple of ways to think about…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 am ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ] There are a couple of ways to think about President Trump ’s predictably failed effort to bar certain news organizations from the White House — if you have to think about it at all.

One version — if you ascribe the “walls-are-closing-in” school of Trumpology — is that as Trump’s second term stacks failure upon failure and Republicans brace for humiliating midterm losses, the president is lashing out.

The other version — if you ascribe to the “four-dimensional chess” view — is that the president is making a point to the American people about the profound bias of the mainstream press and rattling the cages of the media at the same time.

The first view would be more persuasive if we knew that Trump really thought he was failing and really believed that his team was about to get skunked. We’ve seen reporting that, behind closed doors , the president shares his adviser’s sober assessment of his political situation. Really, though? When Trump tried to overturn the election he lost in 2020, was he lying in an attempted self-coup or just delusional? Maybe a little of both, depending on the day. But certainly we know a core Trump attribute is the creation and diligent maintenance of a surreality in which he is always “WINNING.”

The “four-dimensional chess” point of view would be more convincing if it had not been subsequently reported that a background briefing arranged by the White House for reporters with Vice President Vance was the source for one of the articles listed in the president’s grievances against the briefly banned organizations. Whatever else the short-lived press ban was, it was not some strategic masterstroke.

But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t targeted at an audience beyond Washington.

Every day seems to bring another story of another Republican — from MAGA stalwarts like Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) in his Florida gubernatorial race to former Trump skeptics like Michele Tafoya in her Minnesota Senate run — looking to create distance between themselves and the president. Beyond these specific wiggles, the increasing effort in the GOP to be both for and against the Iran war at the same time speaks to the change.

In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll , the percentage of voters who said they “strongly approve” of Trump’s job performance clocked in at 24 percent. That’s far better than the core support Trump’s predecessor, former President Biden , was enjoying when he was getting similarly abysmal overall ratings and the strong support of just 12 percent of voters — sometimes even less.

Indeed, the loyalty of Trump’s core voters has been his political superpower. In his first term, his top-line numbers faltered frequently, but his base mostly stayed with him. And so it is again. If you go back before the Iran war that has tanked Republican ratings across the country, strong approval is basically identical : 25 percent. Or go back to early last year when the brief honeymoon Trump enjoyed with the broader electorate still hadn’t entirely worn off: About the same at 28 percent strong approval .

Good times or bad times. Cheap gas or $5 a gallon. “Drain the swamp” or a big beautiful ballroom built by Beltway bandits. That quarter of the electorate are his people through it all. And that’s why he has such absolute power over the GOP — or at least had it. You can’t win a general election with 25 percent of the voters, but you sure can win a ton of low-turnout primaries.

Wasting time on kicking out the reporters the president doesn’t like probably means very little to persuadable voters, for good or ill. As is often said in Washington, bad behavior from the president is “priced in.” It takes something more than just revoking press passes to get noticed after a decade of Mr. Outrageous.

But Trump knows his people and what they want. And like all super fans, they want him to play the hits. Fighting with cable TV hosts is always triple-platinum in the Trump catalog. When times are tough and the new material isn’t landing, go back to the classics.

The problem for Trump and his party right now is that the president can’t or won’t try to reach any other voters. He and his quarter of the electorate are in a “Love Island” villa together, deeply in love and disconnected from the rest of political reality. In there, it’s always election night 2024 and the vibes are impeccable.

For Republicans who have to live outside of the villa — which is to say every Republican candidate in the country outside of the 10 or so reddest states — the need to find some way through the increasingly difficult climate of this fall is causing them to, for the first time in many cases, publicly break with the president.

Since all the primaries are over, Trump’s ability to punish dissent is not quite over but certainly very much diminished. And if you’re in a race where squishy Republicans and swing voters outnumber Trump’s golden quarter, you’ve got to make a move.

After a split decision in 2022, are independent voters ready to pick a side in this year’s midterms?

If the 2026 midterms are mainly a battle of the two parties’ base voters, Democrats have a lot of reasons to be hopeful. Primary turnout is a strong indicator for election enthusiasm, and Democrats beat Republicans in turnout by an 11-point margin this season.

But a wave the size of the one Democrats are dreaming of requires both a cranked-up base and a dominant performance with persuadable voters, typically found in the growing pool of Americans who aren’t affiliated with either party.

The most recent New York Times/Siena poll has independents breaking for Democrats by 23 points on the generic ballot. For comparison, the same pollsters found a 1-point advantage for Republicans in September of 2022.

That was pretty close to the final result four years ago. AP VoteCast data showed independents actually broke for Democrats by 4 points. The closeness among independents tell the story of how Republicans’ hopes for a big win in the Biden-era midterm came up short. The GOP base was enough to retake the House but only just barely.

In the midterm year before that, 2018, Democrats won the enthusiasm game with Republicans but also did very well with independents: a 13-point advantage according to AP VoteCast. That’s a more typical performance for the party out of power in a midterm year. Combining a decisive advantage with unaffiliated voters with high base voter intensity is how Democrats helped themselves to a best-in-a-generation performance in the House that year.

That was true in 2014, as well. Republicans won independents by 12 points according to that year’s exit poll as they expanded their already substantial House majority of the time and flipped a staggering nine net Senate seats.

If the 23-point edge for Democrats in the latest Times/Siena poll proves predictive, or at least as predictive as their 2022 numbers, the November wipeout for Republicans would be massive. If independents do go for Democrats by 10 points more than they did in 2018, it would be a true tsunami.

But that would require unaffiliated voters not just to show up but resist writing in Fred Rogers or John McCain and actually pick the blue team. Republican messaging that seems mostly aimed at the party’s own base may also help keep frustrated independents from going all the way to the other side.

articles.title: Why would New York reelect Kathy Hochul amid her affordability crisis?
articles.summary: New York is, for far too many people, anything but affordable.
articles.body:
Are New Yorkers suffering from Stockholm Syndrome? That’s the only plausible explanation I can think of for why Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) is leading Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman in the polls.

Stockholm Syndrome describes how kidnapping victims sometimes develop an emotional bond with their abductors, and, as in the original case of a 1973 bank robbery and hostage situation in Sweden, defend and even admire their captors. Hochul may be benefitting from such a response today.

The latest Siena survey shows Hochul, a Democrat, ahead of Nassau County Executive Blakeman by 9 points, 50-41. True, her advantage is slipping slightly , but the same poll shows that 65 percent of New Yorkers expect the governor to be reelected in November.

This makes little sense, with the country so obsessed with “affordability” — why would New Yorkers even consider reelecting the current governor, who has arguably helped make the Empire State one of the least affordable places on earth? According to the World Population Review, New York is the fourth most expensive state in the union overall, also ranking fourth most costly for rents. New York is the 10th most expensive state for groceries, ninth priciest for health care and eighth most expensive for transportation.

In other words, New York is, for far too many people, anything but affordable. Voters should know: it doesn’t have to be this way. Hochul and her disgraced predecessor Andrew Cuomo have made a series of decisions that have driven costs up, but that could be reversed by a change in leadership.

Let’s start with energy. Yes, the war in Iran has inflated the cost of gasoline and other petroleum products, like diesel fuel , in recent months. But New Yorkers have been staring down rising charges for heating their home and filling their tanks since long before President Trump dropped the first bombs on Tehran.

Pandering to the green lobby, New York state officials decided to ban fracking in 2015 and prevent the construction of natural gas pipelines. This was a colossal error. Natural gas is one of America’s most abundant fossil fuels, and one of the cleanest. Hysteria over the possible harm that could come from fracking drove a knee-jerk decision that has caused long-term pain for New Yorkers. Many have likened the politically expedient choice to Hochul’s recent pause on data center construction , which will cost New Yorkers many jobs.

Neighboring Pennsylvania has enacted no such ban on fracking and currently ranks second in the nation in natural gas production , behind only Texas. That helps explain why New Yorkers pay on average $98 per month to heat their homes while the residents of Pennsylvania only shell out $82 every month.

It isn’t just natural gas prices that are putting the screws to New Yorkers. Electricity prices, at 29 cents per kilowatt hour in June, are also through the roof. That compares with 22 cents in Pennsylvania and, for reference, 15 cents in Florida . The suffocating expense of electricity isn’t due to higher feedstock costs, though that plays a role; it also reflects the damaging impact of New York’s push to cut greenhouse emissions, a move Hochul is trying desperately to reverse.

In 2019 New York legislators passed the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act , meant to reduce emissions by 40 percent from 1990 levels and by 85 percent by 2050. The law also demanded the state switch to 100 percent zero-emission electricity by 2040 . None of these targets could be met without enacting a cap-and-trade program that Hochul claimed would cost New York families more than $4,000 per year by 2031. Not surprisingly, Hochul is moving to postpone these requirements .

It isn’t just energy that has been mishandled in New York. Consider housing. According to an analysis by New York’s own state controller, the Empire State’s housing cost burden relative to income ranks third in the country . New York City rents are among the highest in the nation and continue to climb, despite Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s campaign promises to bring them down. Rents in Manhattan have jumped 10 percent over the last year, reaching an all-time high.

Of course, all prices are subject to the laws of supply and demand, including housing. Cumbersome regulations drive building costs in New York to the highest in the entire world, restricting supply. It costs on average $211 per square foot to build in New York, compared to $160 in Florida, even as the Sunshine State is experiencing a once-in-a-lifetime building boom.

Why are all these comparisons so damaging for New York? According to a report from the nonpartisan Citizens Budget Commission out earlier this year, “New York’s business environment is already challenging, ranking the 10th worst state for starting small businesses, 3rd slowest in average growth in small businesses, and the 2nd most regulated state in the nation.” Those regulations translate into higher costs, which, along with sky-high taxes, get passed along to consumers.

Given that affordability is currently voters’ No.1 issue, how can anyone reelect a governor who has delivered high prices and appears determined to continue along the same path? Hochul knows she’s vulnerable on this score. That’s why she’s trying to hoodwink voters by sending payments to help defray soaring utility costs to low- and mid-level income households, right before the election. Some would call that bribery.

Those checks may please some voters, but they should know that New York cannot afford those payments. As wealthy residents and businesses continue to leave the state, the burden of paying for those handouts will fall on the people who remain, either through direct taxation or ever-higher business taxes.

Spending in New York is out of control, and Hochul is doing nothing to rein it in. But you can’t run a scam forever. Let’s hope time runs out on the governor this November.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.
